newsitem.title: CHINA: China confirms date for yuan convertibility.
newsitem.headline: China confirms date for yuan convertibility.

text.p: China confirmed on Thursday it would make its currency convertible under the current account from December 1.

The official Xinhua news agency quoted central bank governor Dai Xianglong as saying that China would accept current account convertibility under the International Monetary Fund's Article VIII from that date.
The IMF said on Wednesday that China had informed it of the decision.
China has been dismantling curbs on the currency's conversion, removing in July restrictions on current account sales of foreign exchange to foreign enterprises.
Beijing has been saying that the yuan was basically convertible on the current account and that it would make full compliance with IMF Article VIII before the end of the year.

"Starting December 1, China will undertake the obligations set forth in the number two, number three and number four clauses of Article VIII of an agreement of the International Monetary Fund...," Xinhua quoted Dai as saying in a letter to the IMF.
The news agency quoted an official of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, as saying that the move reflects Beijing's increased ability to exert macro-economic controls.
It said the action also showed the Chinese government was able to manage its international payments through indirect macro-economic controls and maintain the stability of the currency.
The current account convertibility will help create favourable conditions for China's foreign trade and for foreign investment in China, it said.

Xinhua quoted IMF managing director Michel Camdessus as saying the yuan's convertibility on the current account -- which includes trade, labour and tourism as well as short-term banking and credit facilities -- represented another milestone in China's effort to integrate itself with the world economy.

Article VIII is an undertaking to refrain from imposing restrictions on the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions, or from engaging in discriminatory currency arrangements, according to the IMF.
Xinhua said that in addition to capital account curbs on payments on direct investment, restrictions would remain in place on international loans as well as securities trading.
Chinese still cannot buy or sell foreign exchange freely nor make payments in foreign exchange freely, the agency added.
